lesson.title: Where Wires Meet: The Node and Kirchhoff's Current Law
lesson.summary: Defines a node as a point of common electrical connection between two or more circuit elements, and introduces Kirchhoff's current law, that the currents entering a node must equal the currents leaving it.
lesson.body:
You already know current as the rate of charge flow through a conductor, and that idea leads naturally to an important structural concept for describing circuits: the node. A node is any point in a circuit where two or more components connect to each other. More precisely, every point connected by ideal, zero resistance wire, with no component in between, counts as the same single node, even if that wire bends, branches, or is drawn stretching across an entire page of a schematic. A node is a location of shared electrical connection, not a single physical dot.

Nodes matter because charge cannot be created, destroyed, or accumulated at an ordinary connection point during steady state operation. Whatever current flows into a node from its connected branches must exactly equal whatever current flows back out through the others, an idea called Kirchhoff's current law, or KCL. This is the same conservation of charge principle that guarantees equal current throughout a simple series loop, generalized now to handle points where three, four, or more branches meet rather than just two.

Picture a node where three wires meet: one branch carries 2 amps into the node, a second branch carries 0.5 amps into the node, and a third branch is the only path left for that current to exit. By KCL, the sum of currents in must equal the sum of currents out, so 2 + 0.5 = I_out, meaning the third branch must carry 2.5 amps away from the node. If a fourth branch existed and you already knew it carried 1 amp out, the remaining unknown branch would have to supply whatever difference keeps the books balanced, illustrating how KCL turns unknown currents into simple arithmetic once enough of the picture is known.

Identifying nodes correctly is a foundational skill because most systematic circuit analysis techniques are literally built around them. Nodal analysis, a method introduced later, involves assigning an unknown voltage variable to every node in a circuit relative to a chosen ground reference, then writing one KCL equation per node to solve for all of them simultaneously. Series and parallel circuit rules, which you have already learned, are really just shortcuts that fall directly out of applying KCL and Ohm's law at the nodes of those particular simple structures.

A common early mistake is treating every visually separate wire segment on a schematic as its own node, when in fact several segments connected only by plain wire, with no component between them, are electrically the same node and must be labeled as one. Practicing this identification on paper circuits, tracing every wire until you hit a component, is one of the fastest ways to build the intuition needed for every circuit analysis technique that follows.

It is also useful to notice that the two node case, where exactly two branches meet, is really just the series circuit rule in disguise: with only one way in and one way out, KCL forces the current entering to equal the current leaving, which is precisely why every element along a single series path carries the same current. Once three or more branches share a node, that simple pass through behavior gives way to genuine current splitting, and KCL becomes the tool that tells you exactly how much current each branch carries rather than assuming it must all be equal.
